Least Squares

Fitting, identifiability, computation and estimation

22 teaching sections · 50 worked mathematical/course problems · one explicit authentic examination revisit · 60 final decisions

Source comparison and actual reading · Coverage and verification

1. Sources, prerequisites, and the question being solved

This English author-review draft builds on Orthogonal Projections, Gaussian Elimination, Rank, and Orthogonality. Read those chapters first if a column space, nullspace, orthogonal decomposition or triangular solve is unfamiliar. Calculus is introduced only after an algebraic proof of the central theorem. Statistical extensions state their additional probability assumptions explicitly.

The four primary written courses are MIT 18.06 SC, Gilbert Strang; Stanford EE 263, Stephen Boyd; Berkeley Math 54, Alexander Paulin; and ETH Zurich Linear Algebra for Computer Scientists, Afonso S. Bandeira and Robert Weismantel. Their chapter-specific strengths and limitations were compared before selection. The source audit records actual reading, candidate alternatives and exercise coverage. These are four universities, rather than four pages from one course. Oxford's written numerical-analysis syllabus was screened as an alternative; it is not counted as a fully read fifth course.

Least squares answers a specific optimization question: among vectors produced by a declared linear model, which one is closest to the observed data in a declared norm? It does not establish that the model is scientifically correct, that the data contain no outliers, or that a fitted relation is causal. A model that is linear in unknown coefficients may be nonlinear in its input variable. The algebra below separates those issues so that examination shortcuts have explicit hypotheses.

2. Three spaces and a consistent residual convention

Let A∈ℝm×n and b∈ℝm. The coefficient vector x belongs to ℝn, the fitted observation vector p=Ax belongs to ℝm, and the residual is always r=b-Ax. Stanford uses the opposite residual sign in its slides; that convention has the same squared norm, but signs in intermediate equations must be translated consistently.

Define F(x)=|b-Ax|22. Minimizing the norm or its square gives the same minimizers because squaring is strictly increasing on nonnegative numbers. Multiplying the whole objective by a positive constant also leaves the minimizers unchanged. None of these facts permits changing the relative weights of separate observations.

An overdetermined system has more equations than unknowns. It need not be inconsistent: consistency is exactly b∈col(A). An underdetermined system can also be inconsistent when its rows are dependent and b violates those dependencies. Matrix shape alone establishes neither consistency nor uniqueness.

3. Deriving the normal equations without calculus

Suppose x* minimizes F and consider the line x*+tz for any fixed z∈ℝn. Write r*=b-Ax*. Direct expansion gives

F(x*+tz)=|r*|22-2tzTATr*+t2|Az|22.

If zTATr* were nonzero, a sufficiently small t with the same sign would decrease the objective: the linear decrease dominates the quadratic term. Therefore it must vanish for every z, which is equivalent to ATr*=0. This gives the normal equations

ATAx*=ATb.

Conversely, if those equations hold, the cross term vanishes for every z and

F(x*+z)=F(x*)+|Az|22≥F(x*).

Thus the equations are necessary and sufficient, even when A is rank deficient. This identity proves global minimality. Merely setting a derivative equal to zero without identifying convexity or this nonnegative remainder would leave the sufficiency argument unfinished.

4. Existence, fitted-value uniqueness, and coefficient uniqueness

The column space is a finite-dimensional subspace and therefore has an orthogonal projection. Project b onto it to obtain a unique point p. Since p belongs to the column space, at least one coefficient vector satisfies Ax*=p. The perpendicular residual satisfies AT(b-p)=0, establishing existence for every real matrix and data vector, including A=0.

Two minimizers have the same fitted value. Indeed, the identity in Section 3 applied to their difference gives A(x2-x1)=0. Hence the complete set of minimizers is

x*+kerA.

The coefficients are unique exactly when kerA={0}, equivalently when A has full column rank. This condition is independent of the particular b. If one least-squares problem with this matrix has unique coefficients, every data vector does. A rank-deficient model can have a unique fitted curve on the observed inputs while having infinitely many coefficient descriptions or different predictions at new inputs.

The squared norm of a nullspace component does not affect the fit. Selecting the minimum coefficient norm is an additional optimization criterion, taught explicitly below rather than silently imposed by normal equations.

5. Gram matrices, positive definiteness, and dimensions

For every z,

zTATAz=|Az|22.

Consequently ker(ATA)=kerA and rank(ATA)=rankA. The Gram matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite. It is positive definite, and therefore invertible, exactly when the columns of A are independent. In that case

x*=(ATA)-1ATb,P=A(ATA)-1AT.

The inverse has size n×n, the coefficient map has size n×m, and the projector has size m×m. Dimension checks catch illegal substitutions such as AAT into a formula that requires an invertible column Gram matrix. For a tall full-column-rank matrix, AAT is singular whenever m>n.

The matrix P is symmetric and idempotent. Its range is the column space and its complementary range is the left nullspace. These identities describe observation vectors. They do not mean that x* and b have the same dimension or that the coefficient map is itself an observation-space projector.

6. A complete line fit and two different geometries

Fit bi=c+dti to (1,1),(2,2),(3,2). The design matrix has rows (1,ti), so

ATA=[36614],ATb=[511].

Subtract twice the first equation from the second to get 2d=1. Then 3c+3=5, giving c=2/3, d=1/2. The fitted values are (7/6,5/3,13/6) and residuals (-1/6,1/3,-1/6). Their sum and their time-weighted sum are both zero, so both normal equations are checked. Their squared sum is 1/6.

In the two-dimensional data plot the error segments are vertical: each time is held fixed. In the three-dimensional observation space, the entire vector r is perpendicular to the plane spanned by the constant and time columns. A vertical segment in the data plot is generally not perpendicular to the fitted line. Orthogonal regression, which changes both input and output coordinates to minimize perpendicular plot distances, is a different optimization problem. The interactive figures keep these two geometries separate.

This example reconstructs MIT's published worked fitting example with an independent normal-equation and residual certificate; it is not labeled as an invented examination question.

Vertical response errors and the fitted line

7. Centering, repeated inputs, and intercept identities

For a line with intercept, let t¯=m-1∑iti, b¯=m-1∑ibi, and si=ti-t¯. The design columns 1 and s are orthogonal because ∑isi=0. Provided not all inputs coincide,

d=∑i(ti-t¯)(bi-b¯)∑i(ti-t¯)2,c=b¯-dt¯.

Derive this by writing the line as a+dsi. The first centered normal equation gives a=b¯; the second gives the displayed slope. Transforming back gives c. The denominator is positive exactly when at least two input values differ. Repeated inputs are allowed; complete equality of all inputs destroys separate identifiability of slope and intercept.

An intercept makes the residual sum zero and makes the fitted line pass through (t¯,b¯). These statements require the constant column to be present in the design span. A through-origin model generally has neither property. Centering is an invertible change of coefficient coordinates when the intercept is retained, so fitted values remain unchanged; dropping the intercept after centering the data changes the question unless the transformation is handled explicitly.

8. Beyond lines: bases, polynomials, and identifiability

For chosen functions φ1,…,φn, set Aij=φj(ti). The model is ∑jxjφj(t), linear in x even if the features contain squares, exponentials or trigonometric terms. Least squares fits the sampled feature vectors; it does not require the features to be linear functions of t.

A degree-at-most- k polynomial has k+1 coefficients. Distinct inputs numbering at least k+1 guarantee full column rank: a nonzero polynomial of degree at most k cannot vanish at all those distinct inputs. Repeated samples change weights but do not create new distinct roots. More coefficients than distinct inputs prevent uniqueness, even if the number of observations is large.

Changing basis to A'=AT with invertible T leaves the column space and fitted vector unchanged. Coefficients transform as x'=T-1x. An invertible rescaling of columns therefore changes coefficient norms and numerical conditioning, but not the unpenalized fitted values. A ridge penalty on the new coordinates generally changes the problem because the Euclidean coefficient norm is not invariant under arbitrary basis changes.

For centered symmetric inputs, odd powers are orthogonal to even powers in the discrete sample inner product. The constant and squared-input columns need not be orthogonal: their inner product is ∑iti2, positive unless every input is zero. Centering alone does not diagonalize a polynomial Gram matrix. Construct an actually orthogonal polynomial basis if that property is wanted.

9. QR: solve a triangular system, not an inverse

For full column rank, write the thin factorization A=QR where QTQ=In and R is invertible upper triangular. The normal equations become RTRx=RTQTb. Cancel RT to obtain

Rx*=QTb.

Compute the right-hand side and use backward substitution. The displayed inverse formula R-1QTb characterizes the result; a numerical implementation should solve rather than explicitly form that inverse. Complete Q to an orthogonal matrix [QQ⊥]. Orthogonal norm preservation gives

|b-Ax|22=|QTb-Rx|22+|Q⊥Tb|22.

The first term can be made zero; the second is the irreducible error. Therefore the fitted values are QQTb, the residual is Q⊥Q⊥Tb, and the minimum squared error is |Q⊥Tb|22. Thin Q does not preserve the norm of every vector in the observation space: it extracts coordinates of the projection. The full orthogonal matrix does preserve the norm.

One reflector, then a triangular fit

10. Householder reflection and numerical conditioning

Given a nonzero column segment v, choose α=-sign(v1)|v|2, with sign one when v1=0, and put u=v-αe1. The reflector is H=I-2uuT/(uTu). Since uTu=2(|v|22-αv1), direct substitution gives Hv=αe1. Expanding HTH gives I, so norms are preserved. Apply the same reflectors to b as to A; transforming the matrix alone loses the correct right-hand side. The sign choice avoids subtracting nearly equal large positive numbers in the first component.

For independent columns, the eigenvalues of ATA are the squares of the positive singular values of A. Hence its spectral condition number is κ2(ATA)=κ2(A)2. Forming the Gram matrix can therefore lose accuracy sooner than an orthogonal-factorization method. This is a numerical warning about finite precision, not a claim that exact normal equations are mathematically wrong.

Classical Gram-Schmidt can also lose orthogonality numerically for nearly dependent columns. Householder QR is the standard stable direct route; modified Gram-Schmidt with appropriate reorthogonalization can be useful. A tiny floating-point diagonal does not by itself prove exact rank deficiency. State the tolerance, scaling and data accuracy used in a numerical rank decision. Detailed SVD algorithms belong to the later singular-value chapter; the geometric facts needed here are proved or explicitly identified.

11. Rank deficiency and the minimum-norm convention

Every least-squares solution is x0+z with z∈kerA. Decompose x0=xR+xN into the row space and nullspace. Because these spaces are perpendicular, every solution can be written as xR+w and has squared norm |xR|22+|w|22. Thus the minimum-norm least-squares solution is uniquely the one in the row space.

This defines the Moore–Penrose solution A+b geometrically: first project the data into the column space, then invert the restriction of A from its row space onto its column space. That restriction is injective because a vector both in the row space and nullspace is zero; its dimensions are both the rank, so it is onto. This construction proves existence, uniqueness and linearity without using an invalid inverse of a singular Gram matrix.

For full row rank, the exact minimum-norm solution is ATb' with AATb'=b, hence A+=AT(AAT)-1. For full column rank it is (ATA)-1AT. The two formulas have different rank hypotheses. For arbitrary rank, choose orthonormal bases of the row and column spaces, or use the later SVD construction; do not force either full-rank inverse formula.

Move through nonunique coefficient descriptions

12. Weighted and correlated-error least squares

Let W be symmetric positive definite and minimize (b-Ax)TW(b-Ax). If W=CTC with invertible C, this equals |Cb-CAx|22. Ordinary least squares on the whitened system yields

ATWAx*=ATWb.

For independent columns the coefficient solution is unique. The observation projector is PW=A(ATWA)-1ATW. It is idempotent and satisfies PWTW=WPW; it generally is not symmetric under the ordinary Euclidean product. The residual is W -perpendicular to every design column. If W is diagonal, it rescales individual residual costs. Off-diagonal entries couple residual coordinates, so the loss cannot generally be interpreted as separate independent row weights.

Positive semidefinite weights require another qualification. If CTC=W but C is singular, some observation directions are ignored. Uniqueness requires CA to have independent columns, equivalently ker(CA)={0}. Full column rank of A alone is insufficient. Zero weights remove information and negative weights can destroy convexity or make the objective unbounded below.

Weights change the selected constant

13. Exact linear constraints and feasible nullspace coordinates

Suppose coefficients must satisfy Bx=d. First check feasibility. Choose one feasible x0 and let the columns of Z form a basis for kerB. Then every feasible vector is x0+Zy and the problem becomes

miny|(b-Ax0)-AZy|22.

This reduces the constrained problem to a standard least-squares problem without changing the constraint. Coefficients are unique over the feasible set exactly when kerA∩kerB={0}. There can be redundant constraints; feasibility and independent constraint rows are different properties.

Alternatively stationarity for a feasible minimizer gives ATAx+BTλ=ATb, together with Bx=d, using the Lagrangian F(x)/2+λT(Bx-d). When B has independent rows and the objective is strictly positive along every nonzero feasible direction, the associated block system is nonsingular. Without those hypotheses, multipliers may be nonunique even when the fitted vector is unique. A penalty with a large finite weight approximates a hard constraint; it is not literally the same condition.

Search only along the feasible line

14. Ridge and general quadratic regularization

For λ>0, ridge minimizes |b-Ax|22+λ|x|22. Its normal equations are

(ATA+λI)xλ=ATb.

The matrix is positive definite even when A is rank deficient because its quadratic form is |Az|22+λ|z|22>0 for nonzero z. Equivalently solve the augmented least-squares system with design [AT,λI]T and data [bT,0T]T. This avoids interpreting regularization as new measured observations.

The ridge residual generally does not satisfy ATr=0; instead ATr=λxλ. The fitted-value map is generally not idempotent. With fixed A,b, coefficient norm is nonincreasing as λ increases while unpenalized residual norm is nondecreasing. To prove this, compare optimality inequalities for two positive penalty values and add them; the penalty difference times the coefficient-norm difference has the required sign. Substituting the resulting sign into either inequality controls residuals.

For a penalty λ|Lx|22, uniqueness requires kerA∩kerL={0}. An unpenalized intercept is represented by a zero in the corresponding penalty coordinate; it is not covered by a claim that every coefficient is shrunk. As λ tends to zero, ordinary ridge tends to the minimum-norm least-squares solution; this follows by orthogonally diagonalizing the symmetric Gram matrix and observing the factors 1/(s+λ) on positive eigenvalues, with zero right-hand-side components along its kernel.

The complete regularized objective

15. Fitted values, leverage, and an omitted observation

For full column rank, p=Pb. The diagonal hi=Pii=|Qi,:|22 is a leverage score. Since P is an orthogonal projector, 0≤hi≤1 and ∑ihi=n. Changing only bi by δ changes its own fitted value by hiδ, and changes the full fit by δPei. This is sensitivity to the response at a fixed design; it is not a definition of an outlier.

If removing row i retains full column rank, then hi<1 and the deleted-observation residual at its original input is

bi-aiTx(-i)=ri1-hi.

Here aiT is row i of A. To derive it, let G=ATA, c=ATb and x=G-1c. The deleted normal equations are (G-aiaiT)x(-i)=c-aibi. Subtract the original equations and solve the rank-one correction to obtain x(-i)=x-G-1airi/(1-hi). Multiplication by aiT gives the formula. The same rank-one identity shows that the deleted Gram matrix is nonsingular exactly when 1-hi≠0. At hi=1, deletion loses rank; a zero-over-zero expression is not a valid leave-one-out answer.

Delete one observation and predict it

16. Nested models and exact reductions in error

If one model's column space is contained in another's, the larger model's minimum residual norm cannot increase because it offers every earlier fitted vector. If their orthogonal projectors are P1,P2 with nested ranges, P2-P1 is the projector onto the added perpendicular directions. Thus

|(I-P1)b|22-|(I-P2)b|22=|(P2-P1)b|22.

For one additional feature z, first residualize it against the old model: u=(I-P1)z. If u=0, the feature is redundant and adds no fitted directions. Otherwise the added projector is uuT/(uTu), and the exact error reduction is (uTb)2/(uTu). This gives a fast conceptual solution to many comparison questions without recomputing the complete inverse.

A smaller training residual alone does not prove better prediction on new data. Adding arbitrarily many features can interpolate the sample while making coefficients unstable. That is a limitation of what the optimization criterion measures, rather than a reason to change its mathematical solution.

17. Perturbing observations and nearly dependent features

For fixed full-column-rank A, an observation change δb gives δx=A+δb, δp=Pδb and δr=(I-P)δb. Orthogonal projection is a contraction, so the fitted observation vector and residual change by at most |δb|2. The coefficients can be much more sensitive when columns are nearly dependent because |A+|2 can be large.

For example, Aε with rows (1,1),(0,ε),(0,0) has full column rank for nonzero ε. At data (1,0,1) its coefficients are (1,0) and its residual is (0,0,1). Perturb the second observation by δ; coefficients become (1-δ/ε,δ/ε) while the fitted-vector change is only (0,δ,0). Exact rank and numerical sensitivity are different questions.

If the matrix also changes, differentiating the normal equations gives, to first order,

ATAdx=ATdb+(dA)Tr-AT(dA)x.

The term involving the nonzero residual must not be omitted. Bounds for perturbing both matrix and data need additional residual and scaling information; the simple fixed-design contraction does not justify a universal coefficient-relative-error bound based only on κ(A). A zero true coefficient vector also makes a relative coefficient error undefined.

A small data change and large coefficient changes

18. What the BLUE statement actually assumes

Suppose b=Ax0+ε with fixed full-column-rank A, deterministic unknown x0, E[ε]=0 and covariance σ2I. A linear estimator is Lb. It is unbiased for every x0 exactly when LA=I. Ordinary least squares uses L0=(ATA)-1AT, so it is unbiased and has covariance σ2(ATA)-1.

For any other unbiased linear estimator write L=L0+D with DA=0. The cross products vanish because L0DT=(ATA)-1(DA)T=0. Therefore

Cov(Lb)-Cov(L0b)=σ2DDT.

This is positive semidefinite: every linear combination of coefficient errors has no smaller variance under L than under least squares. No Gaussian assumption is needed for this covariance comparison. The word best refers to the class of linear unbiased estimators under this covariance model; it does not cover every biased or nonlinear estimator, every noise covariance, or every realized sample error.

Stanford's deterministic left-inverse characterization is consistent with zero-noise recovery. The statistical interpretation additionally needs the displayed zero-mean and spherical-covariance hypotheses. With a known positive definite covariance Σ, generalized least squares uses W=Σ-1 and applies the same proof after whitening. With Gaussian errors it also maximizes the corresponding likelihood; that likelihood claim requires the Gaussian model, whereas the unbiased covariance claim does not.

19. Residual degrees of freedom and explicit statistical boundaries

Under the spherical zero-mean noise model, r=(I-P)ε. Its expected squared norm is σ2tr(I-P)=σ2(m-n) for full column rank, because I-P is symmetric idempotent and has rank m-n. This uses E[εTMε]=tr(MCovε) for zero-mean noise, obtained by expanding the double sum.

For arbitrary rank rA, replace n by rA. Dividing residual sum of squares by m-rA gives an unbiased estimator of the common variance only when that denominator is positive and the stated model holds. A saturated fit with rA=m has zero residual but supplies no residual degrees of freedom to estimate noise. Independence of coefficient estimates and residuals requires additional distributional conditions such as joint Gaussianity; zero covariance alone does not prove independence.

With an intercept, the observed data decompose into their constant mean, the centered fitted part, and residual. The latter two are perpendicular, so total centered sum of squares equals explained centered sum plus residual sum. The usual R2 ratio needs nonzero total centered variation. A constant response makes that ratio undefined; forcing a default numerical value would be a software convention rather than the algebraic formula.

A discrete dependence counterexample

20. Complex data and multiple right-hand sides

Over ℂ, use the Hermitian norm and replace transposes by adjoints: A*(b-Ax)=0. Orthogonality and positivity involve z*A*Az=|Az|22, a real nonnegative number. The full-column-rank solution is (A*A)-1A*b. A plain transpose can cancel a nonzero complex column against itself and produce an entirely wrong Gram matrix.

For a data matrix B with several right-hand-side columns, minimize the Frobenius norm |B-AX|F2. This is the sum of the independent column objectives. Solve each with the same factorization; the normal equations are ATAX=ATB in the real case. Uniqueness again depends on the design rank, not on the number of data columns. Reusing QR saves computation without coupling statistically unrelated responses unless an additional joint model is imposed.

21. An implementation that states its contract

For exact rational exercises, elimination on normal equations is useful and transparent. For floating-point computation, use a reliable QR-based solver for independent columns and a rank-aware SVD or pivoted factorization for deficient or uncertain rank. Do not calculate an explicit matrix inverse merely because a theorem displays one.

import numpy as np

def fit_linear_model(design, observations):
    A = np.asarray(design, dtype=float)
    b = np.asarray(observations, dtype=float)
    if A.ndim != 2 or b.ndim != 1 or A.shape[0] != b.size:
        raise ValueError("Use one response for every design row.")
    if not np.isfinite(A).all() or not np.isfinite(b).all():
        raise ValueError("The design and responses must be finite.")
    x, _, rank, singular_values = np.linalg.lstsq(A, b, rcond=None)
    fitted = A @ x
    residual = b - fitted
    return {
        "coefficients": x,
        "fitted": fitted,
        "residual": residual,
        "squared_error": float(residual @ residual),
        "numerical_rank": int(rank),
        "singular_values": singular_values,
    }

The rank is numerical and depends on the solver tolerance; it is not an exact symbolic proof. This solver selects a minimum-norm solution when coefficients are nonunique. The returned residual is computed explicitly because a solver's optional residual array can be empty for rank-deficient or underdetermined inputs; an empty array does not certify zero error. Inspect scaled normal-equation residuals and the model assumptions as well as numerical output.

22. Study route and transfer to unfamiliar questions

First identify the feasible model space, residual sign and metric. Next classify rank and decide whether the requested object is a fitted observation, any minimizing coefficient vector, or the minimum-norm vector. Choose the shortest justified route: a perpendicular certificate, centered sums, a triangular solve, a nullspace parameterization or a precise weighted model. Finally compute the residual and verify the appropriate orthogonality equation and objective value.

The following bank deliberately mixes numerical calculation, proof, inverse construction, counterexamples and model selection. Its source-derived items identify their provenance. The final decisions provide complete mathematical statements and tempting-error diagnoses. Reading solutions supports understanding; timed performance on unseen questions must still be established through later practice. No finite chapter can establish literal universal correctness or guarantee a particular examination result.

Problem 1. MIT's line fit, with a complete error certificate

Course reconstruction: MIT 18.06 SC Session 2.3 worked line fit; independently derived explanation.

Reconstruct the MIT 18.06 SC Session 2.3 worked example: fit a line with intercept to (1,1),(2,2),(3,2). Find coefficients, fitted values and minimum squared error. Explain which perpendicularity is valid.

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

Let A have rows (1,1),(1,2),(1,3) and x=(c,d)T. Its Gram system is 3c+6d=5, 6c+14d=11. Subtracting twice the first equation from the second gives d=1/2, and substitution gives c=2/3. The fitted vector is p=(7/6,5/3,13/6)T. Therefore r=b-p=(-1/6,1/3,-1/6)T and rTr=1/6. Check ∑iri=0 and ∑itiri=0, so ATr=0. For any competing coefficient change z, the squared error is 1/6+|Az|22. Independent columns make equality possible only at z=0. This proves both optimality and uniqueness. The vector residual is perpendicular to the observation-space design plane; individual vertical data-plot errors need not be perpendicular to the plotted line.

Walk through this problem's actual model

Problem 2. Berkeley's nonorthogonal numerical design

Course reconstruction: Berkeley Math 54 Least-Squares Problems, page 2; independently derived explanation.

Independently reconstruct Berkeley Math 54's first example. Let A=[-122-3-13] and b=(4,1,2)T. Find the unique least-squares solution and squared error.

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

Multiplication gives ATA=[6-11-1122] and ATb=(-4,11)T. The determinant is 132-121=11>0, so coefficients are unique. The first equation gives 6x1-11x2=-4; combining the equations yields x2=2, then x1=3. Now Ax=(1,0,3)T and r=(3,1,-1)T. The column products are -3+2+1=0 and 6-3-3=0, independently checking the solve. The squared error is 9+1+1=11. The nonzero residual proves the original system is inconsistent, while the normal system remains consistent. The result is a best observation-space approximation, not an exact solution obtained by discarding an inconvenient equation.

Problem 3. Berkeley's QR example, without an explicit inverse

Course reconstruction: Berkeley Math 54 Least-Squares Problems, pages 3–4; independently derived explanation.

For A=[135110112133] and b=(3,5,7,-3)T, use the Berkeley example's factorization Q=12[1111-1-11-1111-1] and R=[245023002]. Explain every triangular step.

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

The columns of Q each have unit norm and pairwise inner product zero; multiplication verifies QR=A. Directly QTb=(6,-6,4)T. The last triangular equation is 2x3=4, hence x3=2. The second is 2x2+3(2)=-6, hence x2=-6. The first is 2x1+4(-6)+5(2)=6, hence x1=10. Fitted values are (2,4,8,-2)T, so r=(1,1,-1,-1)T and error four. Each design column has zero product with this residual. The nonzero diagonal of R proves full column rank. Thin Q has only three columns in four-dimensional observation space; using QQT=I4 would incorrectly predict zero residual.

Problem 4. Derive the centered slope instead of memorizing it

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

Fit a line to (-1,0),(0,1),(1,3). Derive the slope using centered sums and find the minimum error.

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

The input mean is zero and the response mean is 4/3. The constant and input columns are orthogonal. The centered normal equation for the intercept gives c=4/3. The slope numerator is (-1)0+0(1)+1(3)=3 and its denominator is 1+0+1=2, so d=3/2. Fitted responses are (-1/6,4/3,17/6); residuals are (1/6,-1/3,1/6) and their squares sum to 1/6. Their sum is zero and their input-weighted sum is zero. This also proves that the fitted line passes through (0,4/3), the sample centroid. The coefficients would not be obtained by averaging the three slopes from the origin: a zero input and a free intercept make that shortcut inappropriate.

Problem 5. Removing an intercept changes the optimization

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

Fit a line through the origin to the same three observations as Problem 1. Compare its error with the fit that includes an intercept.

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

There is now one coefficient d, one design column (1,2,3)T, and normal equation 14d=11. Thus d=11/14. The fitted values are (11,22,33)/14 and residuals (3,6,-5)/14. Their input-weighted sum is (3+12-15)/14=0, but their ordinary sum is 4/14, not zero. The squared error is (9+36+25)/196=5/14. The intercept model has error 1/6, and 5/14-1/6=4/21>0. This is consistent with nested model spaces: allowing a free intercept adds possible fitted vectors. The intercept residual-sum identity cannot be used after deleting its design column; doing so would impose a second equation on a one-parameter model.

Problem 6. Repeated inputs and infinitely many line coefficients

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

All three inputs equal two, and responses are 1,4,7. Fit an intercept and slope. Determine all minimizers, their minimum-norm member and the irreducible error.

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

Every fitted value equals c+2d, so only this combination is identified. Minimize (1-a)2+(4-a)2+(7-a)2 over a=c+2d. Completing the square gives 18+3(a-4)2, hence every minimizer satisfies c+2d=4 and has squared error eighteen. The design nullspace is spanned by (-2,1)T. The minimum-norm member lies along the row vector (1,2): write (c,d)=k(1,2) and impose 5k=4. It is (4/5,8/5). Adding any multiple of (-2,1) leaves all fitted responses unchanged. Separate slope estimates are therefore not meaningful from these inputs, although the optimal observed fitted vector (4,4,4) is unique.

Problem 7. A dependent two-column design

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

Let u=(1,2,0)T, A=[u2u] and b=(3,1,2)T. Find every least-squares solution and the unique minimum-norm one.

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

Write a=x1+2x2. The fitted vector is au and the single-column projection coefficient is a=(uTb)/(uTu)=5/5=1. Thus all minimizers satisfy x1+2x2=1. The minimum-norm solution is parallel to (1,2) and equals (1/5,2/5). The fit is (1,2,0), residual (2,-1,2), and error nine. The residual product with u is 2-2=0, which also checks the second column because it is a multiple of the first. The Gram matrix is [5101020] and is singular. Its singularity does not prevent a solution to its normal equations; it prevents using an ordinary inverse and explains nonunique coefficients.

Problem 8. The zero design is a valid boundary case

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

Let A be the zero 3×2 matrix and b=(1,2,3)T. Describe minimizers, fitted values, normal equations and minimum-norm selection.

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

For every x, the fitted vector is zero, the residual is b, and the squared error is 1+4+9=14. Consequently every coefficient vector minimizes the objective. The normal equations reduce to 0=0, agreeing with this complete solution set. The unique minimum-norm vector among all coefficients is zero. The column space is the zero subspace, its orthogonal projector is zero, and the residual projector is the identity. The row space is also zero, consistent with the minimum-norm convention. A program that rejects this model merely because its Gram matrix is noninvertible would incorrectly reject a well-defined optimization problem; a program that reports a unique unrestricted coefficient solution would also be wrong.

Problem 9. Certify an answer by its residual

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

For A=[100111], b=(1,2,4)T, test whether x=(4/3,7/3)T is optimal and unique. Give a global certificate.

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

Its fit is (4/3,7/3,11/3)T, so r=(-1/3,-1/3,1/3)T. The two column products are -1/3+1/3=0, so the normal equations hold. For every change z, the objective is 1/3+|Az|22. This proves global optimality and records the minimum error 1/3. The first two rows of A form an identity matrix, so Az=0 implies z=0, proving uniqueness. This route avoids recomputing an inverse. Merely checking that the candidate approximately satisfies some original equations is insufficient: the residual must be perpendicular to every design column, and uniqueness requires an independent rank argument.

Problem 10. Orthogonal columns that are not normalized

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

Let a1=(1,1,0)T, a2=(1,-1,2)T and b=(1,2,3)T. Find least-squares coefficients and error without forming a dense inverse.

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

Their inner product is zero, while squared lengths are two and six. Each coordinate is therefore its own normalized inner-product ratio: x1=(a1Tb)/2=3/2 and x2=(a2Tb)/6=5/6. The fitted vector is (7/3,2/3,5/3)T, giving residual (-4/3,4/3,4/3)T and error 16/3. As an energy check, |b|22=14, whereas fitted energy is 32/2+52/6=26/3; their difference is 16/3. Using ATb as coefficients would be valid only for orthonormal columns and would omit the required divisions. Orthogonality diagonalizes the Gram matrix but does not make its diagonal equal to one.

Problem 11. One Householder step transforms both sides

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

For A=(3,4)T and b=(1,2)T, construct the stable-sign Householder reflector, solve the transformed problem and recover its minimum error.

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

The column norm is five. Choose α=-5 and u=(8,4)T, giving H=[-3/5-4/5-4/53/5]. Direct multiplication gives HA=(-5,0)T and Hb=(-11/5,2/5)T. The first coordinate is fitted exactly by -5x=-11/5, so x=11/25. The second coordinate cannot be changed and contributes squared error 4/25. Checking in original coordinates, ATb=11 and ATA=25 give the same coefficient. Orthogonality of H preserves the objective, not the data coordinates individually. Applying H only to A while leaving b unchanged would solve a different problem and incorrectly return a different coefficient.

Problem 12. Read irreducible error from full QR

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

A full QR transform gives design [210300] and data (5,6,7)T. Find the coefficients and minimum error without constructing the original orthogonal matrix.

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

Orthogonal transformation preserves the complete residual norm, so the objective is (5-2x1-x2)2+(6-3x2)2+49. Set the second fitted coordinate to six to get x2=2. Then the first gives 2x1+2=5, hence x1=3/2. The remaining term is forty-nine and is independent of the coefficients. Both upper-triangular diagonal entries are nonzero, proving uniqueness. The bottom transformed data coordinate is not an extra equation that the optimizer should force to zero; its design row is identically zero. The original residual vector depends on the omitted orthogonal transformation, but its norm and the coefficient vector are already determined.

Problem 13. A change of feature basis

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

For the line design of Problem 1, replace A by A'=AT where T=[1201]. Find the new coefficients and determine whether fitted values change.

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

The new columns are the constant feature and t+2. Equality of predictions requires ATx'=Ax, so x'=T-1x because A has independent columns. Since T-1=[1-201] and the old coefficients are (2/3,1/2)T, the new vector is (-1/3,1/2)T. Evaluating the new model gives -1/3+(t+2)/2=2/3+t/2, exactly the same fitted line. Hence error remains 1/6. The coordinate values changed because the basis changed; the observation-space subspace did not. This invariance applies to the unpenalized fit. A Euclidean penalty on the new coefficients would generally define a different regularized objective.

Problem 14. A quadratic with a repeated input

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

Fit a0+a1t+a2t2 to (-1,1),(0,0),(0,2),(1,3). Explain why four observations do not make this interpolation exact.

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

At input zero the same fitted value a0 must approximate both zero and two; their squared contribution is a02+(2-a0)2=2+2(a0-1)2. The two other inputs can be fitted exactly once a0 is chosen: require a0-a1+a2=1 and a0+a1+a2=3. The minimum therefore sets a0=1, then subtraction gives a1=1 and either endpoint equation gives a2=1. Error is two, with residuals (0,-1,1,0), perpendicular to each sampled feature column. Three distinct inputs guarantee rank three. The repeated contradictory responses prevent zero error; they provide repeated measurement at one input, not a fourth independent interpolation location.

Problem 15. Why centering does not diagonalize a quadratic Gram matrix

Course-derived conceptual extension: ETH Linear Algebra PartII Example 6.1.4; independently derived obstruction.

In ETH's quadratic-feature construction, can the columns 1,t,t2 have a diagonal Gram matrix at nonzero real inputs merely because the inputs sum to zero? Prove the precise obstruction.

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

The constant and input columns have product ∑iti, which centering makes zero. The input and square columns have product ∑iti3, which vanishes for a symmetric input sample but need not vanish under centering alone. Most decisively, the constant and square columns have product ∑iti2. Every summand is nonnegative; their sum is zero exactly when every input is zero. In that case the last two columns vanish and the design is rank deficient. Therefore no nontrivial full-rank real quadratic design with these raw columns has a diagonal Gram matrix. One can instead subtract the mean square from the squared feature and continue an actual orthogonalization. The statement concerns the chosen basis, not impossibility of orthogonal polynomial fitting.

Problem 16. Unequal observation weights

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

Fit one constant to responses 0,2,4 using weights 1,1,2. Find its weighted error and compare it with the unweighted mean under both objectives.

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

The scalar weighted normal equation is (1+1+2)c=0+2+8, so c=5/2. Its weighted error is 25/4+1/4+2(9/4)=11. The unweighted mean is two, whose weighted error is 4+0+2(4)=12. Thus the weighted optimizer is indeed better for the declared weighted objective. Under the ordinary objective, the mean has error eight, while 5/2 has error 25/4+1/4+9/4=35/4. There is no contradiction: relative row weights changed the objective. A common multiplier on all weights would cancel from the optimizer, whereas doubling only the last weight does not.

Problem 17. A weighted symmetric line fit

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

Fit a line with intercept to (0,0),(1,1),(2,0) with respective weights 1,2,1. Find coefficients and the correct residual orthogonality conditions.

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

The weighted input mean is one, so use centered input s=t-1 with values -1,0,1. Its weighted product with the constant is zero, and with the response it is also zero. The slope is therefore zero. The intercept is the weighted response mean 2/4=1/2. Residuals are (-1/2,1/2,-1/2), giving weighted error 1/4+2(1/4)+1/4=1. Their weighted sum is zero, while the ordinary sum is -1/2 and need not vanish. The weighted time-product is likewise zero. The unweighted intercept would be 1/3 with the same zero slope, but its weighted objective is 1/9+2(4/9)+1/9=10/9>1. The metric, not a changed residual sign, explains the difference.

Problem 18. A nonsymmetric weighted projector

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

Let A=(1,0)T, b=(0,1)T and W=[2112]. Find the weighted fit and show why ordinary perpendicularity fails.

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

The weighted Gram scalar is two, and ATWb=1. Thus x=1/2, p=(1/2,0) and r=(-1/2,1). Multiplication gives Wr=(0,3/2), so ATWr=0. Ordinary ATr=-1/2 is nonzero. The weighted error is rTWr=3/2, smaller than the value two at the ordinary fit x=0. The projector is PW=[11/200]. It squares to itself but is not symmetric; nevertheless PWTW=WPW. The off-diagonal weight couples coordinates, making a purely Euclidean right-angle marker in a plot misleading. This example directly disproves extending symmetric-projector claims to arbitrary coordinate representations of weighted projections.

Problem 19. A full-rank design with zero-weight ambiguity

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

Let A=I2, b=(3,7)T and W=diag(1,0). Does full rank of A imply unique weighted coefficients?

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

The objective is (3-x1)2 because the second residual receives zero weight. It is minimized by x1=3 with arbitrary x2. Thus full rank of the unweighted design does not suffice. With C=diag(1,0), the effective design CA has rank one and nullspace spanned by (0,1), exactly the direction of ambiguity. The minimum weighted error is zero, although a chosen minimizer such as (3,0) has a nonzero ordinary residual. A minimum-norm convention would choose that vector, but the weighted objective alone does not require it. Positive definite weights preserve all observation directions; semidefinite weights may discard some.

Problem 20. Negative weights can destroy existence

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

For A=(1,1)T, b=(0,1)T and signed weight matrix diag(1,-1), determine whether a minimum exists.

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

The proposed loss is x2-(1-x)2=2x-1. It tends to negative infinity as x tends to negative infinity, so no minimizer exists. Here the normal equation degenerates to 0x=-1, which is inconsistent, in contrast with genuine nonnegative least squares where a minimizer always exists. The failure is not caused by having two observations or an overdetermined model; the signed expression is not a squared norm and is not bounded below. Even a stationary point in another indefinite-weight example would need a separate global-minimality test. The usual normal-equation sufficiency proof relies on a nonnegative remainder and cannot be imported after replacing a positive metric by arbitrary signed costs.

Problem 21. Fit subject to an exact coefficient constraint

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

Minimize |(3,0)T-x|22 subject to x1+x2=1. Find the coefficient vector, error and a constraint-based certificate.

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

Parameterize every feasible vector by (t,1-t). The objective becomes (3-t)2+(1-t)2=2(t-2)2+2. Hence the unique solution is (2,-1) and the minimum is two. Its residual is (1,1), parallel to the constraint normal, so it is perpendicular to every feasible direction (z,-z). The unconstrained normal equation r=0 does not hold because its solution (3,0) is infeasible. Instead constrained stationarity is x-b+λ(1,1)T=0 with λ=1. The nullspace-coordinate and multiplier methods agree. The positive quadratic term along all nonzero feasible directions proves uniqueness without requiring an inverse of a larger block matrix.

Problem 22. Check feasibility before optimizing

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

Coefficients must satisfy x1+x2=1 and 2x1+2x2=3. Can a least-squares objective select a feasible solution? Would a large penalty repair the exact problem?

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

Doubling the first equality forces the second left-hand side to equal two, contradicting its required value three. The feasible set is empty, so no constrained minimizer exists for any objective. A finite quadratic penalty on the two constraint violations yields a different unconstrained optimization problem and necessarily leaves at least one violation. Taking a penalty parameter large does not create a point satisfying inconsistent equalities. A numerical solver should report infeasibility or clearly state its relaxation; it must not label the relaxed fit an exact constrained solution. Redundancy of rows would be harmless if right-hand sides were compatible. The contradiction comes from the augmented constraints, not simply from dependence of their coefficient rows.

Problem 23. A constraint can restore uniqueness

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

Minimize (2-x1-x2)2 subject to x1-x2=0. The unconstrained design is rank deficient. Determine the constrained result and justify uniqueness.

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

Feasible coefficients have form (t,t), so the objective is (2-2t)2=4(t-1)2. The unique constrained minimizer is (1,1) and it fits exactly. The unconstrained nullspace is spanned by (1,-1); the constraint's nullspace is spanned by (1,1). Their intersection is zero. Therefore no nonzero feasible direction leaves the fit unchanged, precisely the condition that restores uniqueness. In contrast, imposing x1+x2=2 would make every feasible vector an exact fit and leave a whole line of minimizers. It is the relation between the design kernel and feasible directions that matters, rather than the number of equations called constraints.

Problem 24. Ridge changes both the residual and its certificate

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

With A=I2, b=(3,4)T and penalty λ=1, minimize residual squared plus coefficient squared. Compute both terms and test ordinary residual perpendicularity.

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

The ridge normal equations are 2x=b, so x=(3/2,2). Its residual equals the same vector, and each squared norm is 9/4+4=25/4. The complete objective is 25/2. Ordinary residual orthogonality would require r=0 because A is the identity; it fails. The correct ridge equation is ATr=λx, which holds exactly. The fitted map is Pλ=I/2 and its square is I/4, so it is not a projector. Ridge deliberately accepts some residual in exchange for smaller coefficients. Comparing its unpenalized error with the zero error of ordinary least squares does not evaluate the objective that ridge was asked to minimize.

Problem 25. Ridge on a dependent design

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

Let A=[11], b=2 and λ=2. Find the ridge coefficients, fitted value and complete objective. What happens as the penalty tends to zero?

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

The equations are 3x1+x2=2 and x1+3x2=2. Subtraction gives x1=x2, and then both equal 1/2. The fit is one, residual one, coefficient squared norm 1/2, and complete objective 1+2(1/2)=2. For a general positive penalty, symmetry gives each coefficient 2/(2+λ). As the penalty decreases to zero, both approach one, the minimum-norm exact solution of x1+x2=2. Ridge is unique for every positive penalty because its quadratic form adds a positive cost in the otherwise invisible null direction. Its limiting uniqueness convention should not be misreported as uniqueness of the original unpenalized problem.

Problem 26. A deliberately unpenalized intercept

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

Minimize (2-x1-x2)2+x22. Which coefficient is penalized, and is the optimizer unique despite a rank-one design?

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

Only x2 receives a coefficient penalty. For any fixed x2, choose x1=2-x2 to make the residual zero. The remaining objective is x22, uniquely minimized at x2=0, hence x1=2. The design kernel is spanned by (1,-1), while the penalty kernel is the first coordinate axis; their intersection is zero. Equivalently the augmented design has independent columns. This result does not shrink the unpenalized coefficient toward zero. Replacing the penalty by x12+x22 would give a different problem with a nonzero residual. Statements about ridge shrinking every coefficient require an identity penalty, not a penalty that intentionally exempts an intercept or another known component.

Problem 27. A penalty that fails to identify a missing direction

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

Minimize (1-x1)2+λx12 over (x1,x2) for λ>0. Does a positive penalty parameter alone imply unique coefficients?

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

The objective contains no x2. Completing the square in its only active coordinate gives (1+λ)(x1-1/(1+λ))2+λ/(1+λ). Therefore all minimizers have x1=1/(1+λ) and arbitrary x2, with minimum value λ/(1+λ). Both the design A=[10] and the penalty operator L=[10] vanish on the second coordinate axis. Their common kernel is nonzero, so the augmented design remains deficient. A positive parameter guarantees uniqueness for ordinary identity ridge, but not for every quadratic penalty. A solver's optional minimum-norm output would select x2=0 as an additional convention, not as a conclusion from this loss.

Problem 28. Leverage in a constant model

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

Fit one constant to three responses. Determine the hat matrix, all leverage scores and the response to changing only the first observation by δ.

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

The design is 1=(1,1,1)T and its Gram scalar is three. Hence P=11T/3. Every diagonal entry is 1/3 and their sum is one, equal to the rank. Changing the first response adds δe1 to the data and δPe1=(δ/3)1 to the fitted vector. Thus the first observation changes its own fit by only one third of its change and shifts every other fitted value equally. The full fitted change has norm |δ|/3, no greater than the original perturbation norm |δ|. The leverage scores depend only on the design, not on whether a particular response is unusually large.

Problem 29. Exact deleted-observation errors

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

For a line with intercept at inputs -1,0,1 and responses 0,1,0, compute leverage and leave-one-out residuals. Verify the middle result directly.

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

The orthogonal constant and input columns give P=11T/3+ttT/2. Its diagonal is (5/6,1/3,5/6). Symmetry gives fit (1/3,1/3,1/3) and residual (-1/3,2/3,-1/3). The deleted residual formula gives (-2,1,-2) after division by (1/6,2/3,1/6). Directly deleting the middle observation leaves two endpoints with response zero, hence line zero and middle prediction zero; its deleted residual is one. Deleting the left endpoint leaves the line 1-t, predicting two at input minus one and giving residual minus two. These checks show how leverage amplifies a modest training residual. The denominators are positive because deleting any one point still leaves two distinct inputs.

Problem 30. Leverage one is a rank-loss boundary

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

Let A=[100101] and b=(3,0,2)T. The first leverage is one. Can its deleted-observation error be computed as zero divided by zero?

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

The coefficients are (3,1), fitted values (3,1,1) and residuals (0,-1,1). The first column is e1, so the first observation is fitted exactly for every data vector and has leverage one. Removing its row leaves no information about the first coefficient. Any value of that coefficient minimizes the remaining problem, so the deleted prediction at the omitted input is not uniquely identified. The ratio r1/(1-h1)=0/0 is undefined and does not imply zero prediction error. A minimum-norm convention after deletion would choose first coefficient zero and give residual three, but that answer needs the additional convention. The ordinary full-rank deletion formula explicitly excludes this boundary.

Problem 31. Quantify the gain from adding a slope

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

At inputs -1,0,1 with responses 0,1,3, compare the constant-only and intercept-plus-slope errors. Derive the reduction from an orthogonal added feature.

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

The constant-only fit is 4/3 and its error is 02+12+32-3(4/3)2=14/3. The centered input t=(-1,0,1) is already perpendicular to the constant, so its added coefficient is tTb/(tTt)=3/2. Problem 32. A redundant feature adds coefficients but no fit

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

Add the feature 21 to a model containing only 1, for arbitrary data b∈ℝm with m>0. Determine the gain in error and the coefficient ambiguity.

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

The new fitted vectors are (x1+2x2)1, the same one-dimensional space as before. The optimal fitted constant is b¯, so the gain in minimum error is zero and all coefficient pairs satisfy x1+2x2=b¯. Residualizing the new feature against the old model gives u=(I-P)(21)=0. The one-feature gain formula must therefore use its redundant-feature branch; substituting zero into a denominator would be invalid. The minimum-norm pair is (b¯/5,2b¯/5), an optional convention. Problem 33. Residualize before computing an added-feature gain

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

Start with a constant model on b=(1,0,3)T and add z=(0,1,0)T. Find the exact reduction in squared error and the new fitted values.

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

The old mean is 4/3. The residualized feature is u=z-1/3=(-1/3,2/3,-1/3)T, with squared norm 2/3 and uTb=-4/3. Its added coefficient is -2 and the error reduction is (16/9)/(2/3)=8/3. Problem 34. Perturbations inside and outside the model space

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

Fit A=(1,1)T to b=(1,3)T. Compare perturbations δb=(1,1)T and δb=(1,-1)T.

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

The original coefficient is two, fit (2,2) and residual (-1,1). The coefficient map is the row (1/2,1/2). The first perturbation changes the coefficient by one, changes the fitted vector by (1,1) and leaves the residual unchanged. It lies in the model's column space. The second perturbation has zero mean, so it changes the coefficient and fitted vector by zero and changes the residual by (1,-1). It lies in the perpendicular space. This decomposition explains why a substantial data perturbation can leave coefficients unchanged: sensitivity depends on direction, not just magnitude. A general perturbation splits uniquely into these two perpendicular types.

Problem 35. Stable fitted values with unstable coefficients

Original mathematical/conceptual problem; independently derived solution.

Let Aε=[110ε00], ε=1/1000, and b=(1,0,1)T. Change only the second response by 1/100. Compute the original and new coefficients and explain the contrast.

Read the complete mathematical construction and checks

For nonzero epsilon the first two rows form an invertible triangular block, so those coordinates are fitted exactly; the third response is irreducible residual one. Initially x2=0 and x1=1. After the change, the second equation gives x2=(1/100)/(1/1000)=10 and the first gives x1=-9. The coefficient change is (-10,10) despite a data change of norm 1/100. Yet the fitted change is exactly (0,1/100,0) and the residual remains (0,0,1). Nearly parallel columns allow large canceling coefficients.
